subject: chemistry-2
question: Which change would most likely raise the pH of a bicarbonate-buffered solution that is in contact with a gas phase?

options.text: Bubbling additional carbon dioxide gas through the solution
Adding a measured volume of hydrochloric acid solution
Sweeping dissolved carbon dioxide out of the solution
Adding a neutral salt that does not react with water

explanation:
Dissolved CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, the acid member of the bicarbonate buffer pair. Removing CO2 shifts the equilibrium CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- to the left, lowering H+ and raising the bicarbonate-to-acid ratio, so pH increases. Adding CO2 or a strong acid lowers pH, and an unreactive salt leaves the buffer ratio essentially unchanged.

ELI-10: Dissolved carbon dioxide functions as a hidden acid: combine it with water and carbonic acid forms, which then releases H+. Because that whole sequence is an equilibrium, taking CO2 away pulls the reaction backward and consumes H+, so the pH climbs. This is exactly the chemistry behind hyperventilation raising blood pH and hypoventilation lowering it, since ventilation controls how much CO2 stays dissolved.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
